title: IP Routing on Cisco IOS: The Routing Table, Static and Default Routes, and Inter-VLAN Routing
intro: IP routing is the process by which a Layer 3 device looks up a packet's destination address in a routing table and forwards it toward the next hop, which is what lets traffic leave one subnet or VLAN and reach another. This lesson teaches you to read the IOS routing table, configure static, default and floating static routes, build inter-VLAN routing with router-on-a-stick, SVIs and routed ports, and troubleshoot the classic failures that break it.

sections.heading: What a router does and what the routing table contains
sections.content:
A router is a Layer 3 device whose job is to move packets from one IP network to another. Think of a regional postal sorting office: it does not care who a letter is addressed to personally, it reads only the postcode, looks up which outbound truck serves that area, and hands the letter over. A router does the same with the destination IP address and its routing table.

For every packet the router runs the same sequence. It receives a frame and confirms the destination MAC is its own, strips the Layer 2 header, reads the destination IP, finds the best matching entry in the routing table, decrements the TTL (dropping the packet and sending ICMP time exceeded if it reaches zero), and builds a brand new Layer 2 frame addressed to the next hop. The IP addresses stay the same end to end (ignoring NAT), but the MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop. That rewriting is also why a router separates broadcast domains: a broadcast frame dies at the router interface.

The routing table (the RIB) is built from three kinds of source:

- Directly connected networks. When an interface has an IP address and is up/up, IOS installs a C route for the subnet and an L (local) /32 route for the interface address itself. Shut the interface or lose carrier and both entries vanish.
- Static routes, entered by an administrator with the ip route command.
- Dynamic routes, learned from a routing protocol such as OSPF, EIGRP or RIP.

A router only knows what it has been told. Two routers cabled back to back know the link between them and nothing about each other's LANs until someone adds a static route or enables a routing protocol. This is the single most common beginner misunderstanding.

This lesson assumes you already know how to compute subnets and what NAT does (see the lesson on IP addressing, subnets and NAT), and that VLANs already exist on your switches (see the switching lesson).

The questions to ask whenever a packet does not arrive: which interface should this packet leave through, is there any matching route at all (including a default), and did the route come from the source I expect? A packet with no matching route and no default route is silently dropped, and the sender typically sees Destination host unreachable from the last router that had no answer.

The first three commands you will use constantly:

```
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route connected
R1# show ip interface brief
```

show ip interface brief tells you whether each interface is up/up and which address it holds. If an interface is not up/up, its connected route will not be in the table, and everything built on that route fails with it.

sections.heading: Reading show ip route: longest-prefix match, administrative distance and metric
sections.content:
Here is a trimmed routing table from a branch router:

```
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 5 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
S        10.1.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.0.0.2
O        10.1.4.0/24 [110/20] via 10.0.0.6, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
O        10.1.4.128/25 [110/30] via 10.0.0.10, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/3
```

Each learned entry carries [AD/metric]. The first number is the administrative distance, the second is the metric.

Step one is always longest-prefix match. The router compares the destination to every route and selects the entry with the most specific matching mask. A packet to 10.1.4.200 matches the /16, the /24 and the /25, so the /25 wins and the packet goes to 10.0.0.10. A packet to 10.1.4.20 matches the /16 and the /24 but not the /25, so it goes to 10.0.0.6. A packet to 10.1.9.9 matches only the /16 and goes to 10.0.0.2. The default route 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything with a prefix length of zero, so it is used only when nothing else matches. You can ask IOS directly:

```
R1# show ip route 10.1.4.200
Routing entry for 10.1.4.128/25
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 30, type intra area
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.0.0.10, from 10.255.255.4, 00:03:11 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/3
      Route metric is 30, traffic share count is 1
```

Administrative distance (AD) is trust. It only matters when two different sources offer a route to the exact same prefix and mask. The lower AD wins. Metric then breaks ties between routes learned from the same protocol, and the meaning of the metric depends on that protocol (hop count for RIP, cumulative cost for OSPF).

| Route source | Default AD |
|---|---|
| Connected interface | 0 |
| Static route | 1 |
| eBGP | 20 |
| EIGRP (internal) | 90 |
| OSPF | 110 |
| IS-IS | 115 |
| RIP | 120 |
| EIGRP (external) | 170 |
| iBGP | 200 |

A frequent misconception is that AD is compared before prefix length. It is not. A /25 learned from RIP (AD 120) beats a /16 static route (AD 1) for a destination inside the /25, because prefix length is decided first. AD and metric only choose among candidates for the same prefix.

What to ask when reading the table: is the most specific route the one I intended, is its next hop reachable, and is a lower-AD source (often a forgotten static route) overriding a dynamic route I expected to be used?

sections.heading: Static routing: configuring ip route
sections.content:
A static route is a manual instruction: to reach this destination network, send traffic here. The syntax is:

```
ip route <destination-network> <subnet-mask> {<next-hop-ip> | <exit-interface>} [<distance>]
```

Consider R1 and R2 joined by 10.0.0.0/30, with R1 at 10.0.0.1 and R2 at 10.0.0.2. R2 has a LAN 172.16.20.0/24 that R1 knows nothing about. On R1:

```
R1(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2
```

There are three flavors. A next-hop route names the neighbor IP (as above). IOS must then do a recursive lookup, finding which interface reaches 10.0.0.2, which it resolves from the connected route. An exit-interface route names only the local interface, for example ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 Serial0/0/0. A fully specified route names both: ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/1 10.0.0.2.

On point-to-point links like serial or tunnels an exit interface alone is fine. On Ethernet it is a pitfall: the router then treats every destination in the route as directly attached to the segment and sends an ARP request for each individual destination address, relying on proxy ARP from the neighbor. It works sometimes, bloats the ARP table and breaks when proxy ARP is off. On Ethernet use a next hop, or the fully specified form.

Verify the result:

```
R1# show ip route static
S        172.16.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.0.2

R1# ping 172.16.20.1
!!!!!
```

A static route is installed only if its next hop is resolvable through an up connected route. If the interface goes down, the static route is withdrawn from the table automatically, which is what makes floating statics possible (next section).

Routing is a two-way street, and this is the pitfall that costs the most hours. R1 now knows how to reach 172.16.20.0/24, but R2 must also know how to reach R1's networks. If R2 lacks a return route, the echo request arrives, the reply is dropped or goes elsewhere, and the ping fails even though the forward path is perfect. Always check both directions. Asymmetric routing, where request and reply take different paths, is legitimate in some designs but is a classic source of trouble with stateful firewalls, which see only half of the conversation.

Other pitfalls: a wrong mask (a /24 route where the real network is /23 leaves half the hosts unreachable), a mistyped next hop that is not on a connected subnet (the route never installs), and forgetting to save with copy running-config startup-config.

Static routing is the right tool for stub networks with exactly one way out, small and stable topologies, a default route toward an ISP, and deliberate overrides. It is the wrong tool where topology changes often, because nobody updates the routes when a link fails.

sections.heading: Default routes and floating static routes
sections.content:
A default route is a static route to the all-zeros network, the shortest possible prefix, so it matches only when nothing more specific does:

```
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
```

Think of it as the instruction: if you do not know where this goes, give it to the ISP. IOS flags it in the table with S* and prints Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0 at the top of show ip route. If that line says Gateway of last resort is not set, any destination missing from the table is dropped. The symptom is usually that internal networks work while the internet does not, or that traceroute dies at the first router. Missing default routes are among the most common causes of lost connectivity at branch sites.

A stub site with one uplink needs nothing more than a default route. The upstream router, in turn, needs specific routes back to the site, which is the return-path rule again.

A floating static route is a backup route given a deliberately worse administrative distance so it stays out of the table while a better route exists. Suppose R1 has a primary ISP link and a cheaper backup ISP link:

```
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 250
```

The first route has the default AD of 1. The second carries AD 250. Both target the same prefix, so the lower AD wins and only the primary is installed:

```
R1# show ip route static
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1

R1# show ip route | include 198.51
(no output - backup route is not installed)
```

If the primary interface goes down, its connected route disappears, the primary static loses its resolvable next hop and is withdrawn, and the AD 250 route is promoted into the table. When the primary returns, the better route preempts the backup again. The word floating comes from the route hovering above the table until needed.

Pick the backup AD carefully. It must be higher than the primary and higher than any dynamic protocol you want to take precedence, for example above 110 if OSPF should win when it is available. If you accidentally give the backup the same AD of 1, IOS installs both and load balances across them, which is almost never what you intended for a backup.

There is an important limit. A plain floating static reacts to the local interface state only. If the primary link stays up/up but the ISP beyond it fails (a common situation with an Ethernet handoff to a provider modem), the primary default route stays in the table and traffic black holes. The remedy is to tie the primary route to a probe using IP SLA and the track keyword, so the route is withdrawn when a remote target stops answering.

sections.heading: Inter-VLAN routing: the problem and the three solutions
sections.content:
Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain and, by design, its own IP subnet. A host in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) cannot send a frame directly to a host in VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24); a Layer 2 switch will never forward between VLANs. Traffic that must cross needs a Layer 3 hop, which means a router function somewhere. There are three ways to supply it.

| Method | Where routing happens | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Router-on-a-stick | One router, one trunk link, one subinterface per VLAN | Cheap, needs only a basic router, simple to read | The single trunk is a bottleneck and a single point of failure; all inter-VLAN traffic hairpins through it |
| Layer 3 switch with SVIs | The switch, one switch virtual interface per VLAN | Wire-speed hardware forwarding, no external link, the usual campus design | Needs a multilayer switch and ip routing enabled |
| Routed port | A physical switch port converted with no switchport | Clean point-to-point L3 link to a router or another L3 switch | Carries no VLANs, only one subnet per port |

The oldest legacy method, one physical router interface per VLAN, does not scale and is not used now.

Router-on-a-stick uses one physical link configured as an 802.1Q trunk on the switch side. On the router, the physical interface is split into logical subinterfaces, each tied to one VLAN tag and holding that VLAN's default gateway address.

Router configuration:

```
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# description Sales VLAN 10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 10
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# description Engineering VLAN 20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0.99
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 99 native
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0
```

Switch side:

```
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
```

The encapsulation dot1q 10 line tells the subinterface which VLAN tag it serves. Typical mistakes: putting an IP address on the physical interface, forgetting no shutdown on it (every subinterface stays down), numbering the subinterface differently from the tag without realizing the tag in the command is what counts, omitting the VLAN from the trunk allowed list, and a native VLAN mismatch between the two ends. Some newer switches accept the trunk encapsulation line only on platforms that support ISL, so omit it if the switch rejects it.

sections.heading: Layer 3 switches: SVIs and routed ports
sections.content:
A Layer 3 (multilayer) switch contains a routing engine in hardware. Instead of a router connected by a trunk, the switch itself holds a virtual interface for each VLAN, called a switch virtual interface (SVI). Each SVI gets an IP address, and that address is the default gateway for every host in the VLAN. Traffic between VLANs is routed inside the switch at wire speed, never leaving through a cable.

The configuration has two parts, and forgetting the first is a classic pitfall:

```
SW1(config)# ip routing
SW1(config)# interface vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
```

By default many Catalyst switches ship with IP routing disabled. Without the global ip routing command, the SVIs can hold addresses and even show up/up, so hosts can ping their own gateway, yet the switch will not forward between them. show ip route on such a switch answers with IP routing not enabled.

An SVI goes up/up only when three conditions hold: the VLAN exists in the VLAN database, at least one access port in that VLAN is up (or a trunk allowing the VLAN is up), and the SVI itself is not shut down. An SVI sitting in up/down state usually means no active port exists in that VLAN, or the VLAN was never created. An SVI stuck at administratively down means somebody forgot no shutdown.

A routed port is a physical switch port converted into a Layer 3 interface with no switchport. It behaves like a router interface: it carries no VLAN and holds one IP address.

```
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
SW1(config-if)# no switchport
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.255.0.2 255.255.255.252
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.255.0.1
```

This is the standard design: SVIs face the user VLANs, a routed point-to-point link faces the edge router or firewall, and a default route points up that link. It avoids creating a VLAN and SVI just to connect to the upstream device, and it keeps spanning tree loops out of the uplink.

Verify with:

```
SW1# show ip interface brief
Interface         IP-Address      OK? Method Status      Protocol
Vlan10            192.168.10.1    YES manual up          up
Vlan20            192.168.20.1    YES manual up          up
GigabitEthernet1/0/24 10.255.0.2  YES manual up          up

SW1# show ip route connected
C        10.255.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet1/0/24
C        192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan10
C        192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan20
```

An SVI connected route (C) is created automatically for each addressed, up/up SVI. Those are the networks the switch can route between with no static routes needed.

sections.heading: The default gateway: how a host decides to leave its subnet
sections.content:
Everything above depends on the host knowing where to send traffic that is not local. That is the job of the default gateway, an IP address on the host's own subnet that belongs to a router interface, subinterface or SVI. It is the host's only exit door.

The host makes one decision per packet. It takes its own IP address and mask, performs a bitwise AND with the destination address, and compares the result to its own network. If the destination is on the same subnet, the host ARPs for the destination itself and sends the frame directly. If it is not, the host ARPs for the default gateway and sends the frame to the gateway's MAC while leaving the destination IP unchanged.

Consider PC1 (192.168.10.50/24) pinging PC2 (192.168.20.60/24) through an SVI switch whose gateways are .1 in each VLAN:

| Hop | Source IP | Dest IP | Source MAC | Dest MAC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PC1 to switch | 192.168.10.50 | 192.168.20.60 | PC1 | SVI Vlan10 |
| Switch to PC2 | 192.168.10.50 | 192.168.20.60 | SVI Vlan20 | PC2 |

The IP addresses never change; the MAC addresses change at each routed hop. That is exactly the rewriting described earlier, and it is why a packet capture on PC1 shows the gateway's MAC, not PC2's.

On a Windows host:

```
C:\> ipconfig
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.50
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.1
```

Common host-side faults: no gateway configured (local traffic works, everything else fails), a gateway outside the host's subnet, a gateway that points to the wrong interface or an address no device owns, and a host mask that is wrong, which makes the host believe a remote host is local so it ARPs for it and never reaches the gateway. A useful rule: if a host can ping its gateway but nothing beyond, the problem is past the gateway; if it cannot even ping its gateway, check VLAN membership, the cable, and the gateway address first.

Broadcasts do not cross the gateway, and that creates a problem for DHCP. A client that has no address yet sends a DHCP Discover as a broadcast to 255.255.255.255. The router will not forward it, so a DHCP server on another subnet never sees it. The fix is DHCP relay, configured with the ip helper-address command on the interface facing the clients. The router receives the broadcast, converts it into a unicast to the server, and inserts its own interface address into the giaddr field so the server can select the scope for that subnet. How the DHCP exchange itself works is covered in the DHCP lesson; here we only need the relay configuration.

```
SW1(config)# interface vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.50.0.5
```

Place the command on the client-facing SVI or subinterface, never on the server side. The pitfalls: the wrong interface, a server IP that has no route back to the relay subnet, no scope on the server for the giaddr subnet, and a typo in the helper address. Note also that ip helper-address forwards several other UDP broadcast services by default, such as TFTP, DNS and NetBIOS, unless filtered.

sections.heading: Static versus dynamic routing: setting up the next lesson
sections.content:
Everything so far was configured by hand. That is manageable with two or three routers but becomes a liability as the network grows. The difference between the two approaches is what happens when something changes.

With static routing, the router does exactly what it was told and nothing else. If the link to the next hop fails but its interface stays up, the route stays in the table and traffic is lost. If you add a new LAN, you must touch every router that needs to reach it. Static routes cost no CPU or bandwidth, are predictable, and are completely invisible to attackers who cannot listen to protocol traffic, which is why they remain right for small sites, stubs and default routes.

With dynamic routing, routers run a routing protocol, exchange information about the networks they know, and each one builds its own table. When a link fails the routers detect it, recompute and converge on a new path without human action. The cost is CPU, memory, bandwidth, configuration complexity, and a new attack surface: a router that accepts routing updates from anyone can be fed false routes unless authentication is used.

| Feature | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration effort | High on large networks | Low once the protocol is running |
| Reaction to failure | None, unless tracked or floating | Automatic reconvergence |
| Resource use | Minimal | CPU, memory, bandwidth |
| Predictability | Total | Depends on protocol and topology |
| Best for | Stubs, small sites, defaults, overrides | Larger or redundant networks |

Routing protocols come in families. Interior gateway protocols run inside one organization: RIP (distance vector, simple, hop count, AD 120), EIGRP (Cisco's advanced distance vector, AD 90) and OSPF (link state, open standard, AD 110). Exterior protocols such as BGP run between organizations. Whatever the protocol, the output lands in the same routing table you have been reading, and the same rules apply: longest-prefix match first, then administrative distance, then metric.

The two worlds are frequently combined. A common pattern is OSPF inside the campus and a static default route at the edge that is redistributed into the protocol so every router learns the way out. A floating static route can also serve as a last-resort backup behind a dynamic protocol, as long as its AD is higher than the protocol's (for example 130 behind OSPF's 110).

What to ask yourself when choosing: how many routers need this route, how often does topology change, and what should happen automatically when a link fails? If the honest answer to the last question is that it should heal itself, you want a dynamic protocol. How OSPF and EIGRP actually build their tables, form neighbors and compute paths is the subject of the next lesson. For now the important point is that a routing protocol is simply another source filling the same table, and that you already know how to read the result.

sections.heading: Worked troubleshooting: two VLANs that cannot reach each other
sections.content:
Scenario: a new campus floor has a Layer 3 switch SW1 with VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24, gateway .1) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24, gateway .1). SW1 connects through a routed port (10.255.0.2/30) to the edge router R1 (10.255.0.1), which also has a server network 10.50.0.0/24. Complaint: PC2 in VLAN 20 (192.168.20.60) cannot ping PC1 in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.50).

Step 1, host side. On PC2, ipconfig shows address 192.168.20.60, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.20.1. The configuration is consistent. Ping the gateway first:

```
C:\> ping 192.168.20.1
Reply from 192.168.20.60: Destination host unreachable.
```

PC2 cannot even reach its own gateway, so the problem sits at or below the gateway, not further out.

Step 2, the gateway interface.

```
SW1# show ip interface brief
Interface         IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Vlan10            192.168.10.1    YES manual up                    up
Vlan20            192.168.20.1    YES manual administratively down down
```

Vlan20 is administratively down: somebody configured the address but never issued no shutdown. Fix it:

```
SW1(config)# interface vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
```

Step 3, is routing actually on?

```
SW1# show ip route
IP routing not enabled
```

This is the second fault. With routing disabled the SVIs cannot forward between VLANs even though both are up/up. Enable it:

```
SW1(config)# ip routing
SW1# show ip route connected
C        192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan10
C        192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan20
```

PC2 can now ping PC1 and its own gateway. The inter-VLAN path is repaired.

Step 4, beyond the switch. Users report that VLAN 10 can reach the server 10.50.0.10 but VLAN 20 cannot. SW1 is routing correctly (test with ping 10.50.0.10 source vlan 20, which uses the VLAN 20 SVI as the source address, and it times out). The forward path works, so check the return path on R1:

```
R1# show ip route static
S     192.168.10.0/24 [1/0] via 10.255.0.2
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
```

R1 has a static route for VLAN 10 only. Echo requests from VLAN 20 arrive at the server and the replies reach R1, which has no route for 192.168.20.0/24 and sends them out the default route toward the ISP, where they are dropped. This is asymmetric reachability caused by a missing return route. The fix:

```
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.255.0.2
```

The repeatable method: confirm the host settings, ping the gateway, check interface status with show ip interface brief, check the routing table on every router in the path in both directions, and use extended ping with a specified source. Work from the host outward, change one thing at a time, and retest after every change.

quiz.question: A router holds a static route 10.1.0.0/16 via R2 (AD 1), an OSPF route 10.1.4.0/24 via R3 (AD 110) and a RIP route 10.1.4.128/25 via R4 (AD 120). Where is a packet for 10.1.4.200 sent?

options.label: To R2, because the static route has the lowest administrative distance
To R3, because OSPF has a better metric model than RIP does
To R4, because the most specific matching prefix wins before distance
It is load balanced equally across R2, R3 and R4 for that address

quiz.explanation: The router selects the route with the longest matching prefix first, and 10.1.4.200 falls inside the /25, which is the most specific entry, so R4 is used. Administrative distance only arbitrates between different sources offering the exact same prefix, so the static route's low AD does not matter here. OSPF versus RIP metric models are irrelevant because the two routes are for different prefixes. Equal-cost load balancing needs identical prefixes and equal cost, which is not the case.

quiz.question: An engineer adds a backup default route toward a second ISP that should only be used if the primary default route disappears. Which configuration achieves that?

options.label: Give the backup default route an administrative distance higher than the primary, such as 250
Give the backup default route an administrative distance of 0 so that it is checked first
Configure the backup route with the same distance so IOS holds it in reserve
Configure the backup route with a longer prefix length than the primary default

quiz.explanation: A floating static route has a higher AD than the preferred route to the same prefix, so it stays out of the table until the better route is withdrawn, then it is promoted automatically. An AD of 0 is reserved for connected interfaces and would make the backup preferred, not reserved. Equal distances cause both routes to be installed and traffic to be load balanced, not held in reserve. Changing the prefix length would turn it into a different, more specific route that would be used all the time.

quiz.question: On a new Layer 3 switch, hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 can each ping their own SVI gateway, but inter-VLAN pings fail and show ip route reports that routing is not enabled. What fixes it?

options.label: Add encapsulation dot1q commands under each SVI so tagged frames are accepted
Configure ip helper-address on both SVIs to forward traffic between the VLANs
Convert the uplink to a trunk and create a subinterface for each of the VLANs
Enter ip routing in global configuration so the switch forwards at Layer 3

quiz.explanation: The SVIs are fine, since hosts reach their gateways, but the switch will not route between them until routing is enabled globally. Encapsulation dot1q belongs to router subinterfaces and is not used under an SVI. The helper-address only relays DHCP and similar UDP broadcasts and has no effect on ordinary routed traffic. Subinterfaces over a trunk are the router-on-a-stick design, which is unnecessary when the switch itself holds the SVIs.

quiz.question: DHCP clients in VLAN 30 get no address. The DHCP server, 10.50.0.5, is on another subnet beyond the Layer 3 switch. Which change is correct?

options.label: Put ip helper-address 255.255.255.255 on the server-facing routed port
Put ip helper-address 10.50.0.5 on the VLAN 30 SVI that faces the clients
Put ip helper-address 10.50.0.5 on every access port that VLAN 30 uses
Add a static route for 255.255.255.255 pointing at the DHCP server

quiz.explanation: Client broadcasts arrive on the SVI facing the clients, so that is where the relay must be configured, converting them to unicast to the server and stamping the SVI address as the relay agent so the server picks the right scope. A helper on the server-facing port never sees the client broadcast, and a broadcast address is not a valid relay target. Access ports are Layer 2 and do not take the command. A route for the limited broadcast address is meaningless because routers never forward it.

quiz.question: In a router-on-a-stick design, VLAN 10 works but VLAN 20 hosts cannot reach their gateway even though subinterface Gi0/0.20 has encapsulation dot1q 20 and an IP address. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The router needs ip routing enabled before subinterface addresses can work
The subinterface number must match the VLAN number of the physical port
VLAN 20 is missing from the allowed list on the switch trunk toward the router
The VLAN 10 subinterface must carry the native VLAN for VLAN 20 to function

quiz.explanation: If the trunk's allowed VLAN list omits VLAN 20, tagged frames for that VLAN never reach the router, while VLAN 10 keeps working. Routers have IP routing on by default, and VLAN 10 already proves the interface is routing. The subinterface number is only a label, because the dot1q tag in the command decides the VLAN. VLAN 20 does not depend on any other VLAN being native; the native VLAN only affects untagged frames.
